content: A blood bank is a facility where blood or its components, collected through blood donation, are stored and preserved for future use in transfusions. In 1915, Richard Lewison of Mount Sinai Hospital in New York introduced the use of sodium citrate as an anticoagulant, which revolutionized blood transfusion by transitioning from direct (vein-to-vein) to indirect methods. That same year, Richard Weil demonstrated that anticoagulated blood could be stored under refrigeration. In 1917, Francis Peyton Rous and J.R. Turner developed a citrate-glucose solution, enabling blood to be stored in containers for several days. This advancement led to the establishment of the first blood depot in Britain during World War I. The depot system, created by a U.S. Army officer, is now recognized as the precursor to modern blood banks. By the mid-1930s, the Soviet Union had developed an extensive network of over 60 large blood centers and more than 500 subsidiary facilities, which stored canned blood and distributed it nationwide. This innovation inspired Bernard Fantus, the director of therapeutics at Cook County Hospital in Chicago, to establish the first hospital blood bank in the United States in 1937. Fantus also coined the term blood bank. Within a few years, hospital and community blood banks became widespread across the U.S. In 1940, Willem Johan Kolff organized the first blood bank in Europe. Around the same time, E. Stetson discovered the Rh blood group system, which was identified as a major cause of transfusion reactions. Later, F. Loutit and Patrick L. Mollison developed the acid-citrate-dextrose (ACD) solution, which reduced the volume of anticoagulant required, allowing for larger blood transfusions and longer storage durations. In 1950, the introduction of plastic bags for blood collection replaced fragile glass bottles. This innovation facilitated the safe and efficient preparation of multiple blood components from a single unit of whole blood. In 1979, the anticoagulant-preservative CPDA-1 was introduced, extending the shelf life of stored blood and improving resource sharing among blood banks. Newer solutions containing adenine further extended the shelf life of red blood cells to 42 days. Red blood cells can also be frozen by mixing them with a glycerol solution to prevent ice crystal formation. Frozen red blood cells have a shelf life of up to ten years, but the process is costly and time-consuming, so only a few blood banks maintain frozen stocks. Plasma, particularly Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP), can be stored for up to a year if kept frozen. Platelets, however, are typically stored at room temperature and have a shelf life of only five days due to the high risk of bacterial contamination. Experimental protocols involving bacteriological screening aim to extend platelet storage to seven days.
